title: Be a person
hook: Hillel: where no one is being a person, strive to be one (Pirkei Avot 2:5)
tomorrow: who's actually wise: the one who knows most, or someone else?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the worker who went home unpaid and still guessed the kind reason. Don't judge until you've stood in their place. In their place.

A bag splits on a crowded train and oranges roll everywhere. Twenty people see it. Each one waits for someone else. Hillel has a line for that exact room. In Pirkei Avot he says: in a place where there are no people, strive to be a person. He doesn't mean an empty room. He means a full room where nobody is acting like one. The Hebrew word is ish, a person, a man. In Yiddish, that kind of person is a mensch.
screen: `TWENTY PEOPLE, ROLLING ORANGES.` → `WHERE NO ONE IS BEING A PERSON...` → `...STRIVE TO BE ONE.`

segments.voice: The Talmud tells how Hillel lived it. There was a man from a good family who had lost everything. The Torah says to lend a poor person sufficient for his need, in that which he wanteth, and this man had been used to riding a horse with a servant running ahead. So Hillel got him a horse and a servant. One day there was no servant to be found. So Hillel, the great sage, ran ahead of the horse himself. That's the teaching. In Judaism, being a mensch isn't a personality trait. It's an obligation, and it includes a person's dignity, not only their bread. And when no one else steps up, the obligation lands on you. Now a neighbor who says something close. In the Gospel of Luke, Jesus tells of a man beaten by thieves and left on the road. A priest passes by on the other side. So does a Levite. A Samaritan stops, binds his wounds, and pays for his care. Jesus asks who was neighbor to the man, and says, in the King James words, "Go, and do thou likewise." Shared: in a place where no one is being a person, one person is. The honest difference: Hillel's saying is about the room you're standing in. Luke's parable answers a lawyer's question, who is my neighbor, and makes a Samaritan the one who shows it; Christians read it as Jesus' teaching on love of neighbor.
screen: `A HORSE, A SERVANT, A LOST FORTUNE.` · `HILLEL RUNS AHEAD HIMSELF.` · `THE SAMARITAN STOPS.` · then, large: `BE A PERSON.`

segments.voice: Take out your phone and think of one person others might have left out lately: someone sick, someone new, someone who went quiet. Write them a short, plain message, no big speech, just that you thought of them, and send it if it feels right.
Be a person: Hillel's charge, where no one is acting like a person, strive to be one.
Your line: be a person, even when the room won't. One more saying this week.

howItsDone: Jews study Hillel's saying in Pirkei Avot; being a mensch, a decent person who steps up, is a common Jewish ideal, and Christians read the Good Samaritan in Luke 10 as a teaching on loving one's neighbor.

notes: 2026-10-15 v3: written new in recipe v3, shape wisdom. Story: Hillel and the poor man of good family (Ketubot 67b); teaching named: decency (being a mensch) as obligation, including dignity. Unity thread: the Good Samaritan (Luke 10:29–37), shared (the one who steps up) and one honest difference (Luke's outsider as model, read by Christians as Jesus' teaching on love of neighbor); no ranking. Hook answers day 1475's question.

Check: 'Yiddish speakers later had their own word for it, a mensch' is a usage note, not an etymology claim; cut if a Keeper prefers. 'Ish' as 'a person, a man' is the plain meaning of the Hebrew in Avot 2:5.
Ketubot 67b: the Talmud says Hillel ran before him three mil; the distance is left out. Deuteronomy 15:8 quoted from KJV; confirm.

Luke 10:37 quoted from KJV ('Go, and do thou likewise.'); the parable summarized. 'The one the listeners least expected' describes the parable's turn (Samaritans and Judeans at odds, cf. John 4:9); a Christian Keeper may want to word it.
The Good Samaritan is fair to the priest and Levite as characters in the parable; no claim is made about Judaism or Jewish law.
Storyline: Ray's pre-op day; Zoe hesitates in a line where nobody helps; Ray's 'well?' look. Theo (who left a strict church) knows the Samaritan story; not named in the lesson.
